title: How an order gets fulfilled
summary: Checkout returns immediately with `202 Accepted`. The real work (charging the card, updating the order) happens asynchronously in a worker that reads from Kafka.

api.desc: Stateless HTTP service. It validates the cart, writes the order as `pending`, and publishes an event. It **never** calls Stripe directly, so checkout stays fast even when payments are slow.

kafka.desc: Topic `orders`, partitioned by `order_id`. Events for one order always land on one partition, so they're processed in order.

worker.desc: Consumer group `fulfilment`. Retries with exponential backoff (1s, 4s, 16s), then parks the event on the dead-letter topic.

dlq.desc: Dead-letter topic. Nothing consumes it automatically. An on-call engineer replays events once the cause is fixed.

flows.label: Happy path
flows.description: A customer clicks **Pay** and everything works.

steps.say: The checkout page sends the cart to the Orders API. The idempotency key means a double-click can't create two orders.
The API stores the order as `pending`. This row is the source of truth, and the event that follows is only a notification.
It publishes an `OrderCreated` event, keyed by `order_id` so every event for this order lands on the same partition.
The customer gets an answer in milliseconds. The UI polls the order status from here on.
A fulfilment worker picks the event up. Offsets are committed **only after** the work succeeds, so a crash just means the event is redelivered.
The worker charges the card, using the order id as Stripe's idempotency key, so redelivery can't double-charge.
The order flips to `paid`. The UI's next poll shows the confirmation screen.

flows.label: Payment keeps failing
flows.description: Stripe is down, or the card is declined over and over.

steps.say: Same start: the worker consumes the event.
…and fails. The worker retries after 1s, 4s and 16s. Retries **block the partition**, which is why there are only three.
After the last attempt, the event and its error go to `orders.dlq` and the partition moves on. Other customers aren't stuck behind this order.
The order stays `pending` in Postgres until someone replays the dead letter. That's the state support sees when the customer asks where their order is.

next: To change the retry policy, edit the backoff schedule in the worker. Keep the total retry time below the consumer's `max.poll.interval.ms`, or Kafka will assume the worker is dead.
To add a step such as sending a receipt email, publish an `OrderPaid` event after the `UPDATE` instead of calling the email service from the worker.
To replay dead letters, consume `orders.dlq` with a one-off script that republishes to `orders`. It's safe because every downstream call is idempotent.
